summary: Can you bring back rocks that may hold clues to ancient life on Mars? Mars Mission Trainer is a browser game for ages 7 to 12 that answers the challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer". You pack a cargo hold of only 20 squares, keep your base and yourself going for five mission days, and explore real Jezero crater terrain. Real NASA DONKI solar-flare records set off the storm warnings, the title screen reads this week's strongest flare live from DONKI, and rock samples only count if you bring them home. On a night with too little power you choose which machines to switch off. You fill your air by hand from a tank, tools that a storm breaks stay broken until you fix them with a spare part, and the mission can fail. The end report lists what you did, what changed, and the real science behind it.
details:
Mars Mission Trainer is a browser game for ages 7 to 12. Your mission: keep your base running for five days, and bring home rocks that may hold clues to ancient life on Mars. It runs in a web browser with no install and no login, in English and Japanese.

How it answers the challenge:

- Life support: four bars (health, oxygen, water, food). You fill your air by hand from a tank, and the mission can fail.

- Power: a battery and solar panels. A dust day gives little light. On a night with too little power, you choose which machines to switch off (lights, the radio, the oxygen maker).

- Radiation: Sun storms come on real dates from NASA DONKI. Outside, a storm breaks tools and makes you drop your samples, so you shelter in the base. Broken tools stay broken until you fix them with a spare part.

- Food: a farm in the base. The days you water it decide the harvest.

- Communication: the title screen shows how long a radio signal takes to reach Mars today, and you call Earth by radio on the last evening.

How it plays: you pack a cargo hold of 20 squares with eight kinds of supplies that do not all fit. You launch from Earth, land, and meet your robot in the base. Each day you work at first-person stations (kitchen, farm, tools, radio, recycle), then walk out onto real Jezero crater terrain built from a HiRISE height model, beside a 3D model of NASA's Habitat Demonstration Unit. You have three sample tubes a day. Fine mud rock is worth the most, and a Guide book explains why with facts from NASA's Perseverance rover. Samples only count when you bring them home, where each tube goes onto a shelf. When a real recorded solar flare sets off a warning, you choose: go home, or take one more. The end report lists what you did, what changed, and the real science behind it.

Real and not real: the game marks NASA facts as REAL and game rules as game rules, and a page called "Real data, and what we changed" lists what we simplified. The title screen reads the strongest Sun flare of the last 7 days live from NASA DONKI, with the time it was read. The storms inside the game come from saved DONKI records.

Tools: plain JavaScript and three.js in the browser, hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Code, 3D models and tests were written with AI tools (Claude Code, Codex) under decisions made by the team; every AI use is recorded. The demo video is real game footage, recorded and edited with code written by AI.

Not yet tested with children: the game was built in two days and we have no play-test record with 7 to 12 year olds.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): solar flare and energetic particle records
NASA Mars Trek: HiRISE and CTX imagery and HiRISE terrain model of Jezero crater
NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance: rock samples, panorama PIA24264, MEDA weather records (PDS)
NASA Mars weather feed: Curiosity REMS UV index; NASA 3D models (Habitat Demonstration Unit, astronaut)
projectRefs: three.js (3D library, with GLTF and Draco loaders); interface sounds by Kenney (CC0); Google Fonts Permanent Marker and Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono (SIL OFL 1.1); JPL Approximate Positions of the Planets
